summary: A white paper outlining general requirements for IPng in selected areas, including transition. It is informational.

eli5.summary: A short list of things the next Internet should handle, including how to switch over.

questions: why is dual stack important for migration
what are black holes in ipng transition
how do smart management tools help during ipng transition
subtitle: Key requirements for switching from IPv4 to the next-generation Internet protocol.

tldr.problem: The Internet is too large to switch from IPv4 to IPng overnight. Users will need years to migrate, and different sites will move at different paces, creating complex deployment challenges.
tldr.mechanism: This white paper outlines eight key requirements for stepwise transition: interworking at every stage, coexistence of IPv4 and IPng, dual-stack hosts that run both protocols, DNS support for both address types, smart code that handles black holes, and management tools to diagnose problems.
tldr.outcome: The transition strategy developed for IPv6 implemented most of these principles, including dual-stack deployment, DNS AAAA records, and address mapping strategies.

facts.label: Required host behavior
facts.value: Dual-stack support for all IPng hosts

facts.label: DNS requirement
facts.value: Dual IPv4 and IPng address records

today: RFC 1671 is an Informational document from August 1994. The IPv6 transition strategy directly implemented many of its recommendations, including dual-stack deployment, DNS AAAA records, and the principle of coexistence without translation.

sections.title: The Long Transition Challenge
sections.content:
The transition from IPv4 to IPng will take years or even decades. Vendors will not coordinate product releases, and sites will run old equipment alongside new equipment for extended periods. Every site will need its own staged transition plan suited to its situation. Only the smallest sites might attempt a single-flag-day cutover, and even then only under pressure from their Internet service providers.

Users view the transition to IPng the way they view changing programming languages or operating systems—with concern about minimizing cost and risk to production. This perspective defines strong constraints on how IPng can be deployed: any combination of IPv4 and IPng hosts and routers must be able to interwork seamlessly, and the transition must not require changes to existing IPv4 hosts or applications.
sections.eli5: You can't just flip a switch and change the whole Internet overnight. Companies will use old Internet for years while trying new Internet, and everything has to work together.

sections.title: Interworking and Coexistence
sections.content:
The fundamental requirement is interworking at every stage and every layer. An IPv4 packet must travel from any IPv4 host to any IPv4 or IPng host through any combination of IPv4 and IPng routers, with zero modifications to the IPv4 hosts. Old IPv4 routers must interwork with IPng routers without modification. An old application that knows only IPv4 must be able to run on an unmodified IPv4 system and communicate with an IPng host on the other side of the network.

Header translation between IPv4 and IPng packets is actively harmful because it creates unrealistic constraints: applications would need to know when they are crossing a translation boundary to limit themselves to IPv4 functionality, and manual administration of translator tables across large sites would quickly become chaotic. Instead, the solution is coexistence: IPv4 and IPng must coexist in the same routers and physical paths, allowing the network infrastructure to migrate to IPng without requiring hosts to update in lock-step.
sections.eli5: Old computers must talk to new computers without anyone changing anything on the old computers. You can't try to translate messages between old and new Internet—that causes chaos. Instead, routers handle both kinds at the same time.

sections.title: Address Mapping and Dual-Stack Hosts
sections.content:
During transition, operators need a simple way to understand what is happening. Therefore, IPng's address space should include a mapping for IPv4 addresses, allowing the IPv4 address of a system to be transformed mechanically into its IPng address, typically by adding a prefix. This prefix can be site-specific or provider-specific, simplifying transition planning for network operators without requiring global coordination.

Large-scale transition without translation is only possible if most hosts can run both IPv4 and IPng simultaneously. Dual-stack hosts are essential: if host A needs to talk to both host B (running IPng) and host C (running IPv4), then either A, B, or C must be able to run both protocols. During transition, all IPng hosts must retain the ability to run IPv4. The dual-stack requirement does not mean duplicate implementations; one stack can encapsulate for the other. Only the site prefix needs configuration in addition to the existing IPv4 address.
sections.eli5: The new Internet should have a way to turn old addresses into new ones by adding a prefix. Computers switching to the new Internet have to keep running the old Internet too, so they can talk to computers that haven't switched yet.

sections.title: DNS, Smart Code, and Management
sections.content:
DNS must support dual-stack operation by returning both IPv4 and IPng addresses for hosts that have been upgraded. However, during transition, the DNS database may not reflect reality: a host listed as IPng-capable might not actually be running IPng at a given moment, or an IPng packet might encounter IPv4-only routers unpredictably. These black holes in the routing space create delivery failures that cannot be diagnosed by knowing addresses alone.

Smart dual-stack code must handle black holes: when DNS returns both address types, the application must be able to try one, fail, and automatically fall back to the other without manual intervention. Without this fallback behavior, dual-stack deployment offers no advantage over translation. Additionally, smart management tools are needed during transition to answer questions like: Where are black holes? Is that host really running IPng today? Why does my IPng route differ from my IPv4 route? These tools are essential for diagnosing the complex failure modes that arise during long-term coexistence.
sections.eli5: Computers ask DNS for both old and new addresses, but DNS might be wrong. Smart software tries one, and if it fails, tries the other. Network administrators need tools to find and fix broken spots in the network.

sections.title: Multicast, ATM, Routing, and Security
sections.content:
IPng must support multicast efficiently, following the architectural rule that no multicast packet should travel twice over the same wire. IPv4's physical broadcast mechanisms (used by protocols like ARP) should be replaced with unicast or multicast wherever possible on large networks. The networking industry is investing heavily in ATM technology, so IPng must have a clear model for running over ATM networks and leveraging their multicast capabilities.

Policy-based routing allows traffic to follow specific paths based on source and destination, enabling network operators to control which lines traffic uses. Detailed accounting must accompany policy routing to track traffic type and volume. Finally, IPng's security model must support improved firewalls in routers. Routers need to bar traffic based on source, destination, and transaction type. This likely requires packets to carry an authenticated trace of the (source, destination, transaction) triplet, which is an extra requirement beyond simple address-based filtering.
sections.eli5: The new Internet needs efficient group messages, must work with new switch technology, should let operators control which wires traffic uses, and must have better security walls to keep bad stuff out.
